Location.text: Primarily Tehran, with the fifth stage (Green Corners) extending to Bam and the Hyrcanian Forests.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Tehran Monoxide is a project for ideation, consultation, and interaction with the citizens of Tehran using cultural, artistic, scientific, and educational tools to create sensitivity and awareness regarding the air pollution crisis. This project started in 2010 and was formed as a long-term, multi-stage process in collaboration with a large number of artists, children, adolescents, students, and fellow citizens. The project was realized in five phases. In the first phase, an educational exhibition was held at the Manzoumeh Kherad Institute for Girls. In the second phase, citizens, children, and young adults aged 4 to 18, documented their positions in confronting the air pollution crisis by photographing the city of Tehran. In subsequent phases, the project expanded to urban spaces, pharmacies, schools, green spaces, and cultural institutions, and ultimately, the fifth phase, titled "Green Corners," was dedicated to educational workshops and collaboration with a botanist.

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: The project was executed in diverse contexts, including urban spaces, exhibitions, and workshops. These contexts included schools, pharmacies, streets, gardens, galleries, educational platforms, and green spaces. The selection of these spaces instead of official galleries was done with the aim of creating a direct connection with the daily lives of citizens and enabling genuine dialogue and participation. Each stage of the project was defined by a specific social space and context. For example, in the school, it was an educational and conversational project. In the pharmacy, it led to a dialogue between people and artists, and in urban spaces, it expanded to taking care of plants and daily interaction around them. The space was not only the execution site but also part of the process of creating meaning and communication.

Exhibition locations include: Negarestan Garden, Silk Road Gallery, Manzoumeh Kherad Complex, Qasr Garden Museum, Enghelab Street, CCA Warsaw, Zohreh No Pharmacy, ZK/U (Berlin), Depo (Istanbul), and a Seminar at the Department of Environment.
Workshops took place in: Aaeen Mehr 2 School, Manzoumeh Kherad Complex, Biloba Greenhouse, Book Garden Children's Cafe, Darzikola Village, Bam Orphanage Center, and a caravanserai in Bam.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: The project originated from Farajiani's personal concern regarding Tehran's air pollution and its impact on her son's health. She wanted to see, "As an artist, mother, and citizen, how far can my agency go?" Her goal was to create an experimental platform for dialogue, collective reflection, and action around this issue. The project sought to raise questions about the relationship between citizens, the city, and the environment, and through participation, dialogue, and collective care, to rethink the connection between "art, city, and daily life." At the same time, the project was formed in response to official institutions' lack of attention to the environmental crisis and the lack of opportunity to discuss it. Farajiani consciously distanced herself from official spaces and galleries to create a context where dialogue with citizens and students, rather than exhibition for an elite audience, was at the center. This decision was also a response to the state's severe suppression and control of social and environmental activism during that era, which made any gathering or collective action risky.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: The project faced numerous obstacles: Lack of institutional support, mandatory supervision from the Ministry of Education, political sensitivities toward environmental activities, and social pessimism regarding artistic work. Even some parents criticized her presence in the school, saying "We send our kids to learn math". Additionally, some galleries considered her work "non-standard" because it was executed in schools and non-gallery spaces. To continue working within these limitations, the artist consciously avoided overt political action and viewed "caution as a form of care." By choosing everyday and non-political spaces, focusing on dialogue and education, and maintaining participants' trust, she was able to continue the project. Not relying on official institutions and emphasizing personal relationships and informal networks was also a key strategy for the project's continuation.

Additionally, in 2015 (1394 SH), a selection of these photos was exhibited at the Center for Contemporary Art, Warsaw. sections.title: About the Artist

Artist Biography:

Negar Farajiani (born 1977, Yazd) is a multidisciplinary artist and independent curator whose work focuses on the connection between humans and space, the body, memory, and the environment, as well as individuals and their society. Growing up in the desert city of Yazd shaped her sensitivity towards sustainability, interdependence, and the relationship between humans and place. Using textiles, video, sculpture, and participatory projects, she creates spaces where viewers transform into active participants within a living network of human relationships. She began her career with painting and graphic design, subsequently expanding into participatory and social practices that challenge dominant narratives and highlight often-overlooked communities. Through exhibitions, public artworks, workshops, and lectures both in Iran and abroad, Farajiani continues to build pathways for dialogue and collective presence, bridging local histories with global conversations.

Participation in the project was designed as an open and multi-stage process. The project was built on horizontal communication, intergenerational dialogue, and a focus on shared care and responsibility. Instead of emphasizing the result or product, the process of interaction and collective learning was central - an example of "art as social action" that redefined the relationship between education, environment, and the city.
Project audiences & participants can be categorized into the following groups.

In the first phase, artists helped expand the project's idea by joining it and participating in the dialogues formed around it, whether through presenting artworks or collaborating in the exhibition process. In the second phase, students initially attended the exhibition as visitors, but with the release of a photography open call, they joined the project by submitting their photos of Tehran. This participation resulted in gathering a two-year visual archive of children and Young adults' perspectives on the city. Then, in collaboration with the Kherad Art House, an exhibition of these photos was held, and prizes were awarded to a number of students. A portion of these photos was exhibited at the Center for Contemporary Art, Warsaw in 2015. In the third phase, the project continued with the direct participation of Dr. Torabi, a pharmacist and led to an exhibition of photographs by various artists in a pharmacy in central Tehran, creating a space for encounter and dialogue among citizens regarding the air pollution. In the fourth phase, in collaboration with Nazanin Shivaei, the project expanded to urban and green spaces, including Negarestan Garden, Enghelab Street, and other public spaces; the collaboration emerged with institutions such as the KAF Foundation and the Department of Environment. In the fifth phase, titled "Green Corners," the project focused on holding workshops in schools, the Bam Orphanage Center, a caravanserai in Bam, and Darzikola village. This phase was executed in collaboration with the Biloba Greenhouse, botanists, and student participants. It concluded with an extensive exhibition at the Silk Road Gallery. At this stage, student participation became so prominent that the artist's role shifted to the role of a collaborator in the educational process.
